prompt: A senior bluntly says a junior's PR is 'a mess'. It stings, but the junior notices one real point: the PR mixes three unrelated changes.
tells: the junior notices one real point
why: Bad delivery can still carry a useful point.
trap: The useful part is what they act on.

prompt: A manager gets feedback that she 'micromanages'. Most of it doesn't fit, but she admits she does rewrite reports' emails before they're sent.
tells: Most of it doesn't fit, but she admits
why: Find the true part even when most feels wrong.
trap: Conceding is in an argument; this is filtering feedback.

prompt: An angry customer's review is full of exaggeration, but the product lead pulls out one valid complaint: the export button is hidden.
why: Exaggerated feedback can still contain a fix.
trap: It's not about calming the customer.

prompt: A rival team lead criticizes an architect's design in public. The architect dislikes the tone, but asks himself, 'What part of this would I agree with if a friend said it?'
tells: 'What part of this would I agree with if a friend said it?'
why: Separate the message from the messenger.
trap: A steelman restates their argument to them; he's mining it for himself.

prompt: A report feels her rating was unfair. After a day, she lists the criticisms and marks the one that she'd hear again from anyone.
tells: marks the one that she'd hear again from anyone
why: Look for what's true even in unfair feedback.
trap: No follow-up conversation yet; she's sorting what's true.

prompt: In an interview, asked about unfair feedback, a candidate says they still looked for the 10% that was true and worked on that.
tells: looked for the 10% that was true
why: Use what's true, drop the rest.
trap: It's not about defending or arguing back.
